\title{Blogs about the Paper: "DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models"}

# Meet GRPO: The New Way to Train AI Without Breaking Your GPU Budget

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for pushing Large Language Models (LLMs) beyond simple pattern matching into genuine reasoning capabilities. However, the gold standard for RL in this space, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), comes with a steep price tag. It requires training a separate "critic" model—a value function approximator—that runs alongside the main policy model. This dual-model architecture doubles the memory footprint and computational cost, often making it prohibitive for researchers and organizations working with limited hardware budgets.

Enter DeepSeekMath, a recent paper that introduces a game-changing alternative called Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By rethinking how we calculate advantages during training, GRPO eliminates the need for a dedicated critic model entirely. This innovation not only slashes resource requirements but also delivers state-of-the-art performance in mathematical reasoning, allowing a 7-billion parameter model to rival giants like GPT-4 and Gemini-Ultra on competition-level benchmarks.

## The Bottleneck of Traditional PPO

To understand why GRPO is such a significant leap forward, we first need to look at what makes PPO so demanding. In traditional PPO, the goal is to maximize a reward signal while keeping the model's updates stable. To achieve this stability, PPO relies on an "advantage" function, which tells the model how much better or worse a specific action was compared to the average expectation.

Calculating this advantage traditionally requires a value function, often implemented as a separate neural network known as the critic. This critic estimates the expected return for every single token generated by the policy model. Because this critic must be of comparable size to the policy model itself and must be trained continuously alongside it, the memory overhead becomes massive. Furthermore, since LLMs typically receive rewards only at the very end of a generation sequence (outcome supervision), training a token-level value function accurately is notoriously difficult and computationally inefficient.

DeepSeekMath addresses these inefficiencies head-on by asking a simple question: Do we really need a separate model to estimate values if we can compare outcomes directly?

## How GRPO Works: Comparing Groups Instead of Predicting Values

GRPO solves the critic problem by shifting from individual prediction to group comparison. Instead of maintaining a separate value function to estimate baselines, GRPO samples a group of $G$ different outputs (responses) from the current policy model for every single input question $q$. Let's call these outputs $\{o_1, o_2, \dots, o_G\}$.

Once these candidates are generated, they are scored by a reward model to get rewards $\{r_1, r_2, \dots, r_G\}$. Rather than trying to predict what *should* happen next like a critic does, GRPO simply normalizes these rewards within the group. It calculates the mean ($\mu$) and standard deviation ($\sigma$) of the rewards in that specific group and uses them as the baseline. The advantage for any token in output $o_i$ is derived directly from how its final reward compares to its peers in that group:

$$ \hat{A}_{i,t} = \frac{r_i - \text{mean}(\mathbf{r})}{\text{std}(\mathbf{r})} $$

This approach effectively treats other samples from the same prompt as dynamic baselines. If an output performs better than the average of its siblings in the group, it receives positive reinforcement; if it performs worse, it gets penalized. Because this calculation happens on-the-fly using only the sampled outputs and their scores, there is absolutely no need to train or store a heavy critic model. This reduction in architectural complexity translates directly into significant savings in VRAM usage and training time.

## Performance That Punches Above Its Weight Class

The removal of the critic might sound like a compromise that sacrifices performance for speed, but DeepSeekMath proves otherwise. The authors applied GRPO to their DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B model using only chain-of-thought data from GSM8K and MATH datasets for reinforcement learning fine-tuning. The results were strikingly effective across both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

On GSM8K, which tests grade school arithmetic reasoning via word problems, GRPO boosted accuracy from 82.9% with just supervised fine-tuning to an impressive 88.2%. Even more remarkable was the performance on MATH, a competition-level benchmark covering topics ranging from algebra to combinatorics without external tools or voting mechanisms. Here, GRPO lifted accuracy from 46.8% to 51.7%. When combined with self-consistency checks over 64 samples per query (generating multiple answers and taking the majority vote), DeepSeekMath-7B achieved 60.9% accuracy on MATH—a figure that approaches closed-source leaders like Gemini-Ultra despite having fewer parameters than most competing open models by orders of magnitude.

Beyond pure math scores, GRPO demonstrated excellent generalization. The model showed improvements on Chinese mathematical benchmarks like CMATH (rising from 84.6% to 88.8%), suggesting that optimizing reasoning logic transfers well across languages even when training data is English-centric during RL phases. The algorithm also proved robust enough to work with process supervision (rewarding intermediate steps) as well as outcome supervision (rewarding final answers), offering flexibility depending on data availability and annotation costs.

## Why This Matters for Open Source AI Development

The introduction of GRPO represents more than just an incremental optimization; it lowers the barrier to entry for high-quality AI development significantly before now required massive clusters of GPUs just to run PPO efficiently because of memory constraints imposed by parallel critics).
